title: De Anima
author: Tertullian
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0275.stoa010.opp-lat2, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: uisa est quidem sibi et ex sacris, quas putant, litteris hausisse, quia plerosque auctores etiam deos existimauit antiquitas, nedum diuos, ut Mercurium Aegyptium, cui praecipue Plato adsueuit, ut Silenum Phrygem, cui a pastoribus perducto ingentes aures suas Midas tradidit, ut Hermotimum, cui Clazomenii mortuo templum contulerunt, ut Orpheum, ut Musaeum, ut Pherecydem Pythagorae magistrum. quid autem, si philosophi etiam illa incursauerunt, quae penes nos apocryphorum confessione damnantur, certos nihil recipiendum quod non conspiret germanae et ipso iam aeuo pronatae propheticae paraturae, quando et pseudoprophetarum meminerimus et multo prius apostatarum spirituum, qui huiusmodi quoque ingeniorum calliditate omnem faciem saeculi instruxerint?
passages.english: It [philosophy] has indeed seemed to itself to have drawn also from what they regard as sacred writings, because antiquity thought most of its authors gods, let alone divine men: such as the Egyptian Mercury, with whom Plato was especially familiar; such as the Phrygian Silenus, to whom, when he had been brought to him by shepherds, Midas handed over his own huge ears; such as Hermotimus, to whom the Clazomenians dedicated a temple after his death; such as Orpheus, such as Musaeus, such as Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras. But what if the philosophers also assailed those writings which among us are condemned by being acknowledged as apocryphal, since we are certain that nothing is to be received which does not agree with the genuine prophetic provision, itself already brought forth in [that] age, since we remember both the false prophets and, much earlier, the apostate spirits, who have furnished the whole face of the world with the cunning of such talents as well?
passages.notes: 'certos' is read as 'certi' (we being certain). 'paraturae' (provision/equipment) is an uncertain reading; the sense of the whole sentence is difficult.

passages.original: habuit et philosophia libertatem ingenii et medicina necessitatem artificii ad extendendos de anima retractatus; late quaeruntur incerta, latius disputantur praesumpta. quanta difficultas probandi, tanta operositas suadendi, ut merito Heraclitus ille tenebrosus uastiores . caligines animaduertens apud examinatores animae taedio quaestionum pronuntiarit: terminos animae nequaquam inuenies omnem uiam ingrediens. Christiano autem paucis ad scientiam huius rei opus est.
passages.english: Philosophy has had the freedom of genius, and medicine the necessity of its craft, for extending treatises on the soul; uncertain things are widely investigated, presumptions more widely disputed. As great as the difficulty of proving is the labour of persuading, so that the famous obscure Heraclitus, noticing the vaster darkness among the examiners of the soul, rightly declared from weariness with the questions: you will never find the limits of the soul, though you travel every road. But the Christian needs few things for the knowledge of this matter.
passages.notes: A stray point after 'uastiores' in the text has been ignored.

passages.original: alii immortalem negant animam, alii plus quam immortalem adfirmant, alii de substantia, alii de forma, alii de unaquaque dispositione disceptant, hi statum eius aliunde ducunt, hi exitum aliorsum abducunt, prout aut Platonis honor aut Zenonis uigor aut Aristotelis tenor aut Epicuri stupor aut Heracliti maeror aut Empedoclis furor persuaserunt. deliquit, opinor, diuina doctrina ex Iudaea potius quam ex Graecia oriens.
passages.english: Some deny that the soul is immortal, others affirm that it is more than immortal; some dispute about its substance, others about its form, others about each of its arrangements; these derive its condition from one source, those lead its departure off in another direction, according as the dignity of Plato, or the vigour of Zeno, or the consistency of Aristotle, or the stupor of Epicurus, or the gloom of Heraclitus, or the frenzy of Empedocles has persuaded them. The divine teaching erred, I suppose, by arising from Judaea rather than from Greece.

passages.original: fortasse an exstruentur magis ad auferendam animae corpulentiam, si non alios e contrario inspexerint et quidem plures corpus animae uindicantes. nec illos dico solos qui eam de manifestis corporalibus effingunt, ut Hipparchus et Heraclitus ex igni, ut Hippon et Thales ex aqua, ut Empedocles et Critias ex sanguine, ut Epicurus ex atomis, si et atomi corpulentias de coitu suo cogunt, ut Critolaus et Peripatetici eius ex quinta nescio qua substantia, si et illa corpus, quia corpora includit, — sed etiam Stoicos allego, qui spiritum praedicantes animam paene nobiscum, qua proxima inter se flatus et spiritus, tamen corpus animam facile persuadebunt.
passages.english: Perhaps they will be better equipped to take away the corporeality of the soul, if they do not look at others on the opposite side, and indeed more numerous, who claim a body for the soul. And I do not mean only those who fashion it out of evident bodily things, as Hipparchus and Heraclitus [do] out of fire, as Hippon and Thales out of water, as Empedocles and Critias out of blood, as Epicurus out of atoms (if atoms too gather bodily masses from their coming together), as Critolaus and his Peripatetics out of some fifth substance, I know not what (if that too is a body, since it encloses bodies); but I also cite the Stoics, who, though they declare the soul to be spirit, almost as we do, since breath and spirit are very close to each other, will nevertheless easily persuade [us] that the soul is a body.
passages.notes: 'exstruentur' (they will be equipped/furnished) is taken in the sense 'be better provided [with arguments]'; the text may be corrupt. 'Hipparchus' as a proponent of the fire-soul is odd; some editors read Hippasus.

passages.original: quo, inquit, digresso animal emoritur, corpus est: consito autem spiritu digresso animal emoritur, ergo consitus spiritus corpus est; consitus autem spiritus anima est, ergo corpus est anima. uult et Cleanthes non solum corporis lineamentis, sed et animae notis similitudinem parentibus in filiis respondere, de speculo scilicet morum et ingeniorum et adfectuum, corporis autem similitudinem et dissimilitudinem capere et animam. itaque corporis similitudini uel dissimilitudini obnoxiam. interim corporalium et incorporalium passiones inter se non communicare. porro et animam compati corpori, cui laeso ictibus uulneribus ulceribus condolescit, et corpus animae, cui adflictae cura angore amore coaegrescit per detrimentum scilicet uigoris cuiusque pudorem et pauorem rubore atque pallore testetur.
passages.english: That, he says, whose departure makes a living being die, is a body; but when the implanted breath departs, the living being dies; therefore the implanted breath is a body; but the implanted breath is the soul; therefore the soul is a body. Cleanthes too holds that a likeness to parents appears in children not only in the features of the body but also in the marks of the soul, from the mirror, namely, of character, talents and feelings; and that the soul too takes on the likeness and unlikeness of the body, and is therefore subject to bodily likeness or unlikeness. Further, that the experiences of corporeal and incorporeal things are not shared with one another. Yet the soul suffers with the body, grieving with it when it is hurt by blows, wounds and sores; and the body with the soul, falling sick with it when it is afflicted by care, anguish and love, through the loss, namely, of its vigour, and bearing witness to its shame and fear by blushing and pallor.
passages.notes: 'Spiritus' here renders Greek pneuma, translated 'breath'. The last clause's syntax ('cuiusque ... testetur') is awkward and possibly corrupt.

passages.original: igitur animam corpus ex corporalium passionum communione. sed et Chrysippus manum ei porrigit constituens corporalia ab incorporalibus derelinqui omnino non posse, quia nec contingantur ab eis (unde et Lucretius: tangere enim et tangi nisi corpus nulla potest res), derelicto autem corpore ab anima hominem affici morte. igitur corpus anima, quae nisi corporalis corpus non derelinqueret, uidetur.
passages.english: Therefore the soul is a body, from its sharing in bodily experiences. But Chrysippus too lends him a hand, laying down that corporeal things cannot at all be abandoned by incorporeal ones, since they are not even touched by them (whence Lucretius too: "for nothing can touch or be touched except body"); but when the body is abandoned by the soul, the man is struck with death. Therefore the soul, which would not abandon the body unless it were corporeal, is seen to be a body.

passages.original: Pertinet ad statum fidei simplicem animam determinare secundum Platonem, id est uniformem, dumtaxat substantiae nomine. uiderint artes et disciplinae, uiderint et haereses. quidam enim uolunt aliam illi substantiam naturalem inesse spiritum, quasi aliud sit uiuere, quod uenit ab anima, aliud spirare, quod fiat a spiritu.
passages.english: It belongs to the rule of faith to define the soul as simple, following Plato, that is, uniform, at least in terms of substance. Let the arts and sciences look to it, and the heresies too. For some hold that another natural substance is in it, the spirit, as though living, which comes from the soul, were one thing, and breathing, which is done by the spirit, another.

passages.original: diuiditur autem in partes, nunc in duas a Platone, nunc in tres a Zenone, nunc in quinque et in sex a Panaetio, in septem a Sorano, etiam in octo penes Chrysippum, etiam in nouem penes Apollophanem, sed et in duodecim apud quosdam Stoicorum, et in duas amplius apud Posidonium, qui a duobus exorsus titulis, principali, quod aiunt ἡγεμονικὸν, et a rationali, quod aiunt λογικὸν, in decem et septem exinde prosecuit; ita in alias ex aliis species diuidunt animam. huiusmodi autem non tam partes animae habebuntur quam uires et efficaciae et operae, sicut de quibusdam et Aristoteles iudicauit.
passages.english: Moreover, it is divided into parts: now into two by Plato, now into three by Zeno, now into five and six by Panaetius, into seven by Soranus, even into eight by Chrysippus, even into nine by Apollophanes, and also into twelve by certain of the Stoics, and into two more by Posidonius, who, starting from two headings, the ruling [part], which they call *hēgemonikon*, and the rational, which they call *logikon*, went on from there to cut [it] into seventeen. Thus they divide the soul into some kinds out of others. But things of this sort will be considered not so much parts of the soul as powers and efficacies and operations, as Aristotle too judged concerning some of them.
passages.notes: 'in duas amplius' (into two more) is odd and may be corrupt; possibly a numeral has dropped out.

passages.original: si enim scrutatorem et dispectorem cordis deum legimus, si etiam prophetes eius occulta cordis traducendo probatur, si dominus ipse recogitatus cordis in populo praeuenit: quid cogitatis in cordibus uestris nequam? si et Dauid: cor mundum conde in me deus, et Paulus corde ait credi in iustitiam, et Iohannes corde ait suo unumquemque reprehendi, si postremo qui uiderit feminam ad concupiscendum, iam adulterauit in corde, simul utrumque dilucet, et esse principale in anima, quo intentio diuina conueniat, id est uim sapientialem atque uitalem (quod enim sapit, uiuidum est) et in eo thensauro corporis haberi, ad quem deus respicit, ut neque extrinsecus agitari putes principale istud secundum Heraclitum neque per totum corpus uentilari secundum Moschionem neque in capite concludi secundum Platonem neque in uertice potius praesidere secundum Xenocraten neque in cerebro cubare secundum Hippocraten, sed nec circa cerebri fundamentum, ut Herophilus, nec in membranulis, ut Strato et Erasistratus, nec in superciliorum meditullio, ut Strato physicus, nec in tota lorica pectoris, ut Epicurus, sed ** quod et Aegyptii renuntiauerunt, et qui diuinarum litterarum commentatores uidebantur, ut et ille uersus Orphei uel Empedoclis: namque homini sanguis circumcordialis est sensus. etiam Protagoras, etiam Apollodorus et Chrysippus haec sapiunt, ut uel ab istis retusus Asclepiades capras suas quaerat sine corde balantes et muscas suas abigat sine capite uolitantes, et omnes iam sciant se potius sine corde et cerebro uiuere, qui dispositionem animae humanae de condicione bestiarum praeiudicarint.
passages.english: For if we read that God is the searcher and discerner of the heart; if also his prophet is proved by exposing the secrets of the heart; if the Lord himself anticipates the thoughts of the heart in the people: 'Why do you think evil in your hearts?'; if David too [says]: 'Create a clean heart in me, O God', and Paul says that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, and John says that each person is reproved by his own heart; if, finally, whoever has looked on a woman to lust [after her] has already committed adultery in his heart: then both things become clear at once, both that there is a ruling part in the soul, to which the divine attention applies, that is, the faculty of wisdom and of life (for what is wise is alive), and that it is kept in that treasury of the body to which God looks; so that you should not think that this ruling part is moved from outside, according to Heraclitus, nor blown through the whole body, according to Moschion, nor shut up in the head, according to Plato, nor rather presiding at the crown, according to Xenocrates, nor lying in the brain, according to Hippocrates, nor yet around the base of the brain, as Herophilus [held], nor in the membranes, as Strato and Erasistratus, nor in the midpoint between the eyebrows, as Strato the physicist, nor in the whole cuirass of the chest, as Epicurus, but [...] what the Egyptians too have reported, and those who were regarded as interpreters of divine writings, as also that verse of Orpheus or of Empedocles: 'For in man the blood around the heart is perception.' Protagoras too, Apollodorus too and Chrysippus hold this view, so that Asclepiades, beaten back even by these, may go looking for his goats bleating without a heart and drive away his flies flying about without a head, and all may now know that those rather live without heart and brain who have prejudged the arrangement of the human soul from the condition of beasts.
passages.notes: The edition marks a lacuna (**) after 'sed'; the sense is presumably 'but in the heart'. 'Strato' appears twice (with Erasistratus, and as 'the physicist'); one occurrence may be an error.

passages.original: inrationale autem posterius intellegendum est, ut quod acciderit ex serpentis instinctu, ipsum illud transgressionis admissum, atque exinde inoleuerit et coadoleuerit in anima ad instar iam naturalitatis, quia statim in naturae primordio accidit. ceterum cum idem Plato solum rationale dicat ut in anima dei ipsius, si nos etiam inrationale naturae adscripserimus, quam a deo anima nostra sortita est, aeque inrationale de deo erit, utpote naturale, quia naturae deus auctor est. sed enim a diabolo inmissio delicti, inrationale autem omne delictum, igitur a diabolo inrationale, a quo et delictum, extraneum a deo, a quo est inrationale alienum.
passages.english: But the irrational element must be understood as later, as having happened from the prompting of the serpent, namely that very act of transgression, and as having from then on become ingrown and grown together with the soul, after the likeness of something now natural, because it happened immediately at the beginning of nature. Besides, since the same Plato calls only the rational [part] as in the soul of God himself, if we also ascribe the irrational to the nature which our soul received from God, the irrational will equally be from God, as being natural, since God is the author of nature. But the instigation to sin is from the devil, and all sin is irrational; therefore the irrational is from the devil, from whom sin also comes, and is foreign to God, to whom the irrational is alien.

passages.original: Conuertor ad intellectualium partem, quemadmodum illam Plato a corporalibus separatam haereticis commendauerit agnitionem ante mortem consecutus. ait enim in Phaedone: quid tum erga ipsam prudentiae possessionem? utrumne impedimentum erit corpus, an non, si quis illud socium assumpserit in quaestionem?
passages.english: I turn to the part concerning intellectual things, how Plato, having attained knowledge before death, commended it, separated from bodily things, to the heretics. For he says in the Phaedo: "What then about the very acquisition of wisdom? Will the body be a hindrance or not, if one takes it as a partner in the inquiry?"

passages.original: Et hic itaque concludimus omnia naturalia animae ut substantiua eius ipsi inesse et cum ipsa procedere atque proficere, ex quo ipsa censetur. sicut et Seneca saepe noster: insita sunt nobis omnium artium et aetatum S\'emina magisterque ex occulto deus producit ingenia, ex seminibus scilicet insitis et occultis per infantiam, quae sunt et intellectus. ex his enim producuntur ingenia. porro et frugum seminibus una generis cuiusque forma est, processus tamen uarii.
passages.english: Here too, therefore, we conclude that all the natural properties of the soul, as belonging to its substance, are inherent in it and proceed and advance together with it, from the time it is itself reckoned [to exist]. As our Seneca too often [says]: "The seeds of all arts and ages are implanted in us, and God, a teacher in secret, draws out our talents"—from seeds, that is, implanted and hidden through infancy, which are also the intellect. For from these talents are drawn out. Moreover, in the seeds of crops too there is one form for each kind, yet the developments vary.

passages.original: nam et hic etiam de locis interest. Thebis hebetes et brutos nasci relatum est, Athenis sapiendi dicendique acutissimos; ubi penes Colyttum pueri mense citius elocuntur praecoca lingua. siquidem et Plato in Timaeo Mineruam affirmat, cum urbem illam moliretur, nihil aliud quam regionis naturam prospexisse talia ingenia pollicitam, unde et ipse in Legibus Megillo et Cliniae praecipit condendae ciuitati locum procurare. sed Empedocles causam argutae indolis et obtusae in sanguinis qualitate constituit;
passages.english: For here too place makes a difference. It is reported that at Thebes people are born dull and stupid, at Athens most acute in wisdom and speech; there, in Colyttus, children speak a month earlier with precocious tongue. Indeed Plato too in the Timaeus affirms that Minerva, when she was founding that city, looked to nothing but the nature of the region, which promised such talents; whence he himself in the Laws instructs Megillus and Clinias to take care over the site for founding a city. But Empedocles placed the cause of a sharp or a dull disposition in the quality of the blood;
passages.notes: Colyttus is a district (deme) of Athens.

passages.original: Quidam de caelis deuenisse se credunt tanta persuasione, quanta et illuc indubitate regressuros repromittunt, ut Saturninus Menandri Simoniani discipulus induxit, hominem affirmans ab angelis factum primoque opus futtile et inualidum et instabile in terra uermis instar palpitasse, quod consistendi uires deessent, dehinc ex misericordia summae potestatis, ad cuius effigiem nec tamen plene perspectam temere structus fuisset, scintillulam uitae consecutum, quae illud exsuscitarit et erexerit et constantius animarit et post decessum uitae ad matricem relatura sit.
passages.english: Some believe that they have come down from the heavens, with as great a conviction as that with which they promise that they will without doubt return there, as Saturninus, the disciple of Menander the Simonian, taught. He affirmed that man was made by angels, and that at first, a worthless, weak and unstable work, he squirmed on the earth like a worm, because he lacked the strength to stand; then, out of the mercy of the supreme power, after whose likeness, though not fully perceived, he had been rashly constructed, he obtained a tiny spark of life, which roused him, raised him upright, animated him more steadily, and after his departure from life will carry [him] back to its source.
passages.notes: "ad matricem": literally "to its mother-source" or "womb"; the referent of the spark's return is somewhat ambiguous.

passages.original: magnae autem ac multae differentiae corporum pro gentilitate, pro magnitudine, pro habitudine, pro aetate, pro ualetudine. num ergo et obliuionum differentiae aestimabuntur? sed uniformis obliuio est; ergo non erit corporalitas multiformis in causa exitus uniformis. multa item documenta teste ipso Platone diuinationem animae probauerunt, quae proposuimus iam Hermogeni. sed nec quisquam hominum non et ipse aliquando praesagam animam suam sentit aut ominis aut periculi aut gaudii augurem. si diuinationi non obstrepit corpus, nec memoriae opinor officiet.
passages.english: But there are great and many differences of bodies, according to race, size, condition, age and health. Will there then also be reckoned differences of forgetting? But forgetting is uniform; therefore bodiliness, which is multiform, will not be the cause of a uniform outcome. Likewise many proofs, by the testimony of Plato himself, have demonstrated the soul's power of divination, which we have already set out against Hermogenes. Indeed there is no human being who does not himself at some time feel his soul to be prophetic, a foreteller of an omen, or a danger, or a joy. If the body does not obstruct divination, neither, I think, will it hinder memory.

passages.original: eam editam et de uteri fornace fumantem et calore solutam ut ferrum ignitum et ibidem frigidae immersum, ita aeris rigore percussam et uim animalem rapere et uocalem sonum reddere. hoc Stoici cum Aenesidemo et ipse interdum Plato, cum dicit perinde animam extraneam alias et extorrem uteri prima adspiratione nascentis infantis adduci, sicut exspiratione nouissima educi. uidebimus an ex sententia sua finxerit. ne ex medicis quidem defuit Hicesius et naturae et artis suae praeuaricator.
passages.english: [They say] that [the infant], once born and smoking from the furnace of the womb and relaxed by the heat, like iron heated red-hot and then plunged at once into cold water, is struck by the chill of the air and so both seizes the animating power and gives out a vocal sound. This is held by the Stoics together with Aenesidemus, and at times by Plato himself, when he says that the soul, being foreign and elsewhere and exiled from the womb, is drawn in with the first breath of the newborn infant, just as it is drawn out with the last exhalation. We shall see whether he devised this according to his own view. Nor among the physicians was Hicesius lacking, a betrayer both of nature and of his own art.
passages.notes: The subject of the first sentence (the newborn) is implied from the preceding context.

passages.original: quodsi qui, ut Plato, perinde non putat duas animas in unum conuenire sicut nec corpora, ego illi non modo duas animas in unum congestas ostendissem, sicut et corpora, in fetibus, uerum et alia multa cum anima conserta, daemonis scilicet, nec unius, ut in Socrate ipso, uerum et septenarii spiritus, ut in Magdalena, et legionarii numeri, ut in Geraseno, quo facilius anima cum anima conseretur ex societate substantiae quam spiritus nequam ex diuersitate naturae.
passages.english: But if anyone, like Plato, thinks that two souls cannot come together into one, just as bodies cannot either, I would have shown him not only two souls gathered into one, as also bodies, in pregnancies, but also many other things joined with the soul, namely of a demon, and not just one, as in Socrates himself, but also of a sevenfold spirit, as in the Magdalene, and of the number of a legion, as in the Gerasene; so that a soul will more easily be joined with a soul, by kinship of substance, than wicked spirits [with a soul], given their difference of nature.

passages.original: at idem in sexto Legum monens cauere ne uitiatio seminis ex aliqua uilitate concubitus labem corpori et animae supparet, nescio de pristina magis an de ista sententia sibi exciderit. ostendit enim animam de semine induci, quod curari monet, non de prima aspiratione nascentis. unde, oro te, similitudine animae quoque parentibus de ingeniis respondemus secundum Cleanthis testimonium, si non et ex animae semine educimur? cur autem et ueteres astrologi genituram hominis ab initio conceptus dirigebant, si non exinde et anima est? ad quam aeque pertinet, siquid est, flatus.
passages.english: But the same [Plato], when in the sixth book of the Laws he warns to beware lest a corruption of the seed from some baseness of intercourse should add a stain to body and soul, has, I do not know whether he has lost hold more of his earlier view or of this one. For he shows that the soul is brought in from the seed, which he warns to be cared for, not from the first breath of the newborn. Whence, I ask you, do we also correspond to our parents in likeness of soul in respect of our mental qualities, according to the testimony of Cleanthes, if we are not also produced from the seed of the soul? And why did the ancient astrologers too calculate a person's nativity from the beginning of conception, if the soul is not also from that point? To which [the soul] equally belongs the breath, if it is anything.
passages.notes: "supparet" (add/attach) is a rare word; the final sentence is compressed and its sense uncertain.

passages.original: cotidie existant, cur solus Pythagoras alium atque alium se recognoscat, non et ego? aut si priuilegium philosophorum est, et utique Graecorum, quasi non et Scythae et Indi philosophentur, cur neminem et retro meminit Epicurus, neminem Chrysippus, neminem Zeno, ne ipse quidem Plato, quem forsitan Nestorem credidissemus ob mella facundiae?
passages.english: [If such souls] arise daily, why does Pythagoras alone recognise himself as one person after another, and not I as well? Or if it is a privilege of philosophers, and of course of Greeks, as though Scythians and Indians did not also philosophise, why did Epicurus remember no one [he had been] before, nor Chrysippus, nor Zeno, not even Plato himself, whom we might perhaps have believed to be Nestor on account of the honey of his eloquence?
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening clause is incomplete.

passages.original: publicorum ipsorumque carcerum licet otiosorum recordentur! perinde qui integre morati commendauerint iudici uitam, quaero praemia, sed potius inuenio supplicia. nimirum magna merces bonis in animalia quaecumque restitui. pauum se meminit Homerus Ennio somniante: sed poetis nec uigilantibus credam. et si pulcherrimus pauus et quo uelit colore cultissimus? sed tacent pennae, sed displicet uox, et poetae nihil aliud quam cantare malunt. damnatus est igitur Homerus in pauum, non honoratus.
passages.english: …let them remember the public [works] and the prisons themselves, however idle! Likewise, as for those who, having lived upright lives, have commended their life to the judge, I look for rewards, but rather I find punishments. A great reward, no doubt, for the good, to be restored into some animal or other! Homer remembers that he was a peacock, as Ennius dreamed; but I would not believe poets even when they are awake. And what if the peacock is very beautiful and adorned with whatever colour it wishes? Yet its feathers are silent, its voice is displeasing, and poets want nothing other than to sing. Homer, therefore, was condemned into a peacock, not honoured.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing from the context before ('if [they compare it with] mines and workhouses and works...').

passages.original: Nulla quidem ad hodiernum dementiae huiusmodi sententia erupit sub nomine haeretico, quae humanas animas refingat in bestias. sed necessarie hanc quoque speciem intulimus et exclusimus ut superioribus cohaerentem, quo perinde in pauo retunderetur Homerus sicut in Pythagora Euphorbus atque ita hac etiam metempsychosi siue metensomatosi repercussa illa rursus caederetur quae aliquid haereticis subministrauit. nam et Simon Samarites in actis Apostolorum redemptor spiritus sancti, postea quam damnatus ab apostolo cum pecunia sua interitum frustra fleuit, conuersus ad ueritatis expugnationem quasi pro solacio ultionis, fultus etiam artis suae uiribus, ad praestigias uirtutis alicuius Helenen quandam Tyriam de loco libidinis publicae eadem pecunia redemit dignam .
passages.english: No opinion of madness of this kind has so far, to this day, broken out under a heretical name, that would refashion human souls into beasts. But we have necessarily brought forward and excluded this form too, as being connected with what preceded, so that Homer might be beaten back in the peacock just as Euphorbus in Pythagoras, and so, this metempsychosis or metensomatosis also being repelled, that [doctrine] might again be struck down which has supplied something to the heretics. For Simon the Samaritan too, in the Acts of the Apostles, the would-be purchaser of the Holy Spirit, after he had been condemned by the apostle and had wept in vain for his destruction together with his money, turned to assaulting the truth as if for the consolation of revenge, and, supported also by the powers of his art, for the illusions of some power, he bought with that same money a certain Helen of Tyre from a place of public lust, a fitting
passages.notes: "redemptor spiritus sancti" literally "buyer of the Holy Spirit". The sentence breaks off at "dignam", continued in the following context ("a fitting reward for himself in place of the Holy Spirit").

passages.original: at ille ei dedit passionem, cuius est actio. quodsi hominis est pati mortem dissolutricem corporis et peremptricem sensus, quam ineptum ut tanta uis ad hominem non pertinere dicatur. multo coactius Seneca, post mortem, ait, omnia finiuntur, etiam ipsa. hoc si ita est, iam et mors ad semetipsam pertinebit, si et ipsa finitur; eo magis ad hominem, in quo inter omnia finiendo et ipsa finitur. mors nihil ad nos, ergo et uita nihil ad nos.
passages.english: But he gave to him the suffering, of which the action is [death's]. Now if it belongs to man to suffer death, which dissolves the body and destroys sensation, how absurd that so great a force should be said not to pertain to man. Much more forcefully Seneca says: after death all things are ended, even [death] itself. If this is so, then death too will pertain to itself, if it also is ended; all the more to man, in whom, among all things being ended, it too is ended. [If] death is nothing to us, then life too is nothing to us.
passages.notes: The first sentence is elliptical; "ille" likely refers to Epicurus, and the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: sicut ergo dignatio dei et in ethnicos, ita et temptatio mali in sanctos, a quibus nec interdiu absistit, ut uel dormientibus obrepat qua potest, si uigilantibus non potest. tertia species erunt somnia, quae sibimet ipsa anima uidetur inducer ee ex intentione circumstantiarum. porro quia non est ex arbitrio somniare (nam et Epicharmus ita sentit), quomodo ipsa erit sibi causa alicuius uisionis? num ergo haec species naturali formae relinquenda est seruans animae etiam in ecstasi res suas perpeti? ea autem, quae neque a deo neque a daemonio neque ab anima uidebuntur accidere, et praeter opinionem et praeter interpretationem et praeter enarrationem facultatis ipsi proprie ecstasi et rationi eius separabuntur.
passages.english: Just as, therefore, God's favour [extends] even to the heathen, so also the temptation of evil [extends] to the saints, from whom it does not withdraw even by day, so that it creeps upon them while asleep as it can, if it cannot while they are awake. The third kind will be dreams which the soul seems to bring upon itself from its attention to its circumstances. Further, since dreaming is not a matter of choice (for Epicharmus too thinks so), how will [the soul] itself be the cause of any vision for itself? Is this kind then to be left to the natural form, the soul keeping even in ecstasy the capacity to undergo its own affairs? But those [dreams] which will seem to occur neither from God nor from a demon nor from the soul, being beyond expectation, beyond interpretation and beyond the power of narration, will be set apart properly for ecstasy itself and its own account.
passages.notes: "inducer ee" is a scanning error for "inducere". The clause "seruans animae etiam in ecstasi res suas perpeti" is obscure; rendering tentative.

passages.original: sed quidam ad immortalitatem animae, quam quidem non a deo edocti infirme tuentur, ita argumentationes emendicant, ut uelint credi etiam post mortem quasdam animas adhaerere corporibus. ad hoc enim et Plato, etsi quas uult animas ad caelum statim expedit, in Politia tamen cuiusdam insepulti cadauer opponit longo tempore sine ulla labe prae animae scilicet indiuiduitate seruatum. ad hoc et Democritus crementa unguium et comarum in sepulturis aliquanti temporis denotat.
passages.english: But some, on behalf of the immortality of the soul, which they defend weakly since they have not been taught by God, beg for arguments in such a way that they would have it believed that even after death certain souls cling to their bodies. For to this end Plato too, although he dispatches whichever souls he wishes to heaven at once, nevertheless in the Republic sets forth the corpse of a certain unburied man, preserved for a long time without any decay, evidently because of the soul's indivisibility [from it]. To this end Democritus too notes the growth of nails and hair in graves for some time.

passages.original: nam etsi prae gaudio quis spiritum exhalet, ut Chilon Spartanus, dum uictorem Olympiae filium amplectitur, etsi prae gloria, ut Clidemus Atheniensis, dum ob historiarum praestantiam auro coronatur, etsi per somnium, ut Plato, etsi per risum, ut P. Crassus, multo uiolentior mors quae per aliena grassatur, quae animam per commoda expellit, quae tunc mori affert, cum iucundius uiuere est in exultatione in honore in requiete in uoluptate.
passages.english: For even if someone breathes out his spirit for joy, like Chilon the Spartan while embracing his son, a victor at Olympia; even if for glory, like Clidemus the Athenian while being crowned with gold for the excellence of his histories; even if in sleep, like Plato; even if through laughter, like Publius Crassus: much more violent is the death that advances through things foreign [to it], that drives out the soul through pleasures, that brings dying at the moment when it is most delightful to live, in exultation, in honour, in rest, in pleasure.

passages.original: Quo igitur deducetur anima, iam hinc reddimus. omnes ferme philosophi, qui immortalitatem animae, qualiterqualiter uolunt, tamen uindicant, ut Pythagoras, ut Empedocles, ut Plato, quique aliquod illi tempus indulgent ab excessu usque in conflagrationem uniuersitatis, ut Stoici, suas solas id est sapientium animas in supernis mansionibus collocant. Plato quidem non temere philosophorum animabus hoc praestat, sed eorum qui philosophiam scilicet exornauerint amore puerorum. adeo etiam inter philosophos magnum habet priuilegium impuritas. itaque apud illum in aetherem sublimantur animae sapientes, apud Arium in aerem, apud Stoicos sub lunam. quos quidem miror, quod imprudentes animas circa terram prosternant, cum illas a sapientibus multo superioribus erudiri affirment. ubi erit scholae regio in tanta distantia diuersoriorum?
passages.english: Where, then, the soul will be led, we now set out from here. Almost all the philosophers who maintain the immortality of the soul, in whatever way they want it, such as Pythagoras, Empedocles, Plato, and those who grant it some time from its departure until the conflagration of the universe, such as the Stoics, place only their own souls, that is, those of the wise, in the dwellings above. Plato, indeed, does not grant this indiscriminately to the souls of philosophers, but to those, of course, who have adorned philosophy with the love of boys. So great a privilege does impurity have even among philosophers! Accordingly, with him wise souls are raised up into the ether, with Arius into the air, with the Stoics under the moon. I am surprised at these, indeed, that they lay the unwise souls low around the earth, while they affirm that these are taught by the wise, who are far above. Where will the place of the school be, with so great a distance between the lodgings?
passages.notes: 'Arius' is probably Arius Didymus, the Stoic doxographer; identification uncertain.
